title: Almighty (CCC 268–278)
hook: God shows his almighty power most of all in mercy

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Creed's shape: Father, Son and Spirit. Your line was three movements. Did you spot the making, the mending and the growing? Today, one word from the Creed's first line. Day one thousand sixty-nine.

What does strength look like? A weightlifter with the bar overhead. A storm that peels a roof off. A fist on a table. Now another scene: a big man down on one knee on a sidewalk, tying a toddler's shoe, careful not to pull the laces too tight. That's strength too, the kind that holds itself back. The Creed calls God the Father almighty. And when the Catechism explains that one word, it makes a claim about where that power shows most. Today's word: almighty.
screen: `A WEIGHTLIFTER. A STORM. A FIST.` → `A MAN TYING A TODDLER'S SHOE.` → `WHERE DOES POWER SHOW MOST?`

segments.voice: Almighty means able to do all things. Mary sings it in Luke's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "he that is mighty, hath done great things to me." But the Book of Wisdom ties that power to something unexpected. Speaking to God, it says: "thou hast mercy upon all, because thou canst do all things." Mercy because of power, not in spite of it. The Catechism pairs the two words of the Creed, Father and almighty, and says they shed light on each other. God's power is a father's power. It's never arbitrary, never a whim. Then the Catechism faces the hard question head on. If God is almighty, why is there so much suffering? It admits that faith in God's power can be put to the test by evil. And its answer is a strange one. It points to the cross, where God looks weakest. Paul calls the crucified Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. Then comes the line behind today's word. The Catechism says God shows his almighty power by turning people from their sins and bringing them back to friendship with him. And it quotes a prayer of the Roman Mass that goes further: that God shows his almighty power most of all by sparing and by showing mercy. That's the carry: power as mercy. On this reading, any force can break things; it takes a deeper power to forgive, and to heal what's broken. The Creed's first adjective, read this way, isn't a threat hanging over the world. It's the strength of someone who can afford to be gentle.
screen: `MERCY UPON ALL, FOR THOU CANST DO ALL.` · `FATHER AND ALMIGHTY TOGETHER.` · `THE CROSS: THE POWER OF GOD.` · `POWER SHOWN MOST IN MERCY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: show strength by being gentle. Settle, and breathe. Think of a moment coming up today when you'll hold a little power. Over a child. A coworker who made a mistake. Someone on a customer service line. A slow driver ahead of you. Picture that moment clearly. Now picture using your power gently: a softer word, a little patience, letting a small offense go. Rehearse it once in your mind, start to finish. If you pray, you can ask God for that kind of strength. If you don't, just hold the picture steady. The bell holds the time.
Almighty. Able to do all things, and, in the Catechism's reading, showing that power above all in mercy and forgiveness. Today's word.
Your line: power as mercy. Today, when the moment you pictured arrives, choose the gentle strength once, and notice what it costs you and what it gives. Day one thousand sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics profess God as the Father almighty in the Creed at Mass, and some of the Church's prayers, including the one the Catechism quotes, address God's power and his mercy together.

myth: the Catechism says God's power is arbitrary
it says it's never arbitrary, and it's joined to his fatherhood.
the Catechism avoids the question of suffering
it admits evil can test faith in God's power, and points to the cross.
a prayer the Catechism quotes says God shows his power most by sparing and showing mercy

fork.setup: the Catechism quotes a prayer of the Mass on how God shows his almighty power most of all. what does it say?
fork.reveal: most of all by sparing and showing mercy. the Catechism adds that God shows his power by turning people from their sins and back to friendship with him.

original.note: Greek: the word the Greek creeds use where English says almighty.

trapdoor: what you thought: almighty means God can do whatever he likes, like a tyrant.
what it means: a power that's never arbitrary, joined to fatherhood, and shown above all in mercy and forgiveness.
what a scholar hears: Wisdom's 'thou hast mercy upon all, because thou canst do all things'; Paul's crucified Christ as the power of God; the Roman collect the Catechism quotes on sparing and mercy.

notes: Confirm Challoner wording of Luke 1:49 and Wisdom 11:24 (Challoner verse numbering).

Catechism paraphrased (copyright): fatherhood and power shed light on each other (CCC 270); power never arbitrary (CCC 271); faith tested by evil, the cross as God's power (CCC 272); power shown above all in forgiving sins and restoring friendship, with the collect (CCC 277). Confirm.
The Missal collect (Latin 'Deus, qui omnipotentiam tuam parcendo maxime et miserando manifestas') is paraphrased in English from the Latin; the current English Missal text is copyrighted.
Hook: 'it makes a claim about where that power shows most' rests on the index hook ('most of all in mercy'), which follows the collect.
Review: 'one word from the Creed's first line' (Father almighty); confirm it reads well for both creeds.
Original: παντοκράτωρ as the Greek creeds' word for almighty; confirm.

Editor: 'above all' / 'most of all' now attributed only to the Missal collect, which says it; CCC 277's own sentence says God shows his power by converting us and restoring friendship (teach and fork). howItsDone's 'often' softened.
